sections.title: Eggs of Kosher Birds
sections.html:
Eggs of kosher birds are permitted to eat, and eggs of non-kosher birds are forbidden to eat, for "what comes from the impure is impure, and what comes from the pure is pure" (Bekhorot 5b). Chicken eggs, which we usually eat, may be bought from anyone, since eggs of non-kosher birds are not found among us; consequently all eggs that resemble the ordinary eggs we consume are presumed kosher (SA 86:2).

If the eggs differ from ordinary eggs, the Sages said (Ḥullin 64a) that if both ends of the egg are rounded, that is, round like a ball; or pointed, that is, elongated; or if the yolk (the yellow) is outside and the white is inside – it is certain that it is an egg of a non-kosher bird, and it is forbidden to eat it. Even if the seller says that it is from a kosher bird, he is not believed. But if one end is rounded and one is pointed, and the yolk is inside and the white outside, it may be from a kosher bird; then, if a person who understands halakha says that it is from a kosher bird, he is relied upon and the egg is kosher. And if he is considered a trustworthy person but does not understand halakha, only if he says that the egg is from a specific species of bird known to be kosher is the egg kosher (see SA and Rema 86:1).

Eggs laid by a female bird that became a tereifa as a result of an injury or illness are forbidden to eat; just as its flesh is forbidden to eat, so its eggs are forbidden to eat. Likewise, an egg found in the innards of a neveila (a bird that died without kosher slaughter) is forbidden to eat.1 One should not place an egg of a tereifa or neveila under a hen to brood on it, lest people mistakenly eat it. But if they placed it and a chick hatched from it, the chick is kosher (SA 86:7; Pitḥei Teshuva 4).

Eggs found inside a female bird after it was slaughtered in a kosher manner are kosher. If they already have a white and a yolk, their law is that of eggs, which are pareve, and it is permitted to eat them with milk. And if they do not yet have a white, their law is that of meat, and it is forbidden to eat them with milk (SA 87:5).

sections.title: Blood in Fertilized Eggs
sections.html:
Blood found in an egg, if it is in the place from which the formation of the chick begins, is subject to the prohibition of blood, and the prohibition spreads to the entire egg. Some say that this blood prohibition is from the Torah: just as the blood of a chick is forbidden by Torah law, so too the blood from which its formation begins is forbidden by Torah law (Rashba and Rosh). And some say that its prohibition is rabbinic, since in practice it is not yet life-blood that sustains a living bird (Rif, Rambam, Ra'ah, Sha'arei Dura).

But if the blood found in the egg is not in the place where the chick's formation begins, it is not forbidden; however, because of mar'it ayin (how it appears to onlookers) it must be removed, and the egg is permitted. This blood appears when one of the blood vessels that envelop the egg tears at the beginning of its formation.

The Rishonim disagreed on the question of where the place is from which the chick begins to form. Some say it is in the inner yellow part of the egg called the "yolk" (Rif, Rambam and SA 66:3). On the other hand, some say that the formation begins in the outer white part called the "white" (Ra'ah and Maharshal). And some say that as long as the blood is at the place of the kesher ha-ḥelbon (the chalaza), that is, in the cord that connects the yolk to the side of the egg, only the blood is forbidden, but the rest of the egg is permitted, since the formation has not yet begun; and when the blood has spread from the kesher ha-ḥelbon to the germ of the yolk, the formation has begun and the whole egg is forbidden (Rashi and Tosafot). In practice, since wherever there is blood in an egg one must be concerned that according to one of the approaches it is blood of formation, which forbids the whole egg, the custom is to forbid the entire egg for any blood found in it (Rema 66:4; Baḥ; Ben Ish Ḥai).

And although the blood of a chick's formation is forbidden, one who wants to eat a hard-boiled egg, or to make a hole in an egg and suck it out, need not check it before eating it, since the vast majority of eggs contain no blood, and we hold the rule that we follow the majority. But if the eggs are opened to make an omelet from them or to mix them into a dish or baked good, since one sees the egg in any case, one should be stringent and look whether it contains blood (Beit Yosef, and SA and Rema 66:8). And since, if blood is found in it, the entire egg will be forbidden, it is worthwhile to check each egg in a separate vessel, so that if blood is found in it, only that egg will be thrown away, and there will be no need to throw away the eggs or the dish mixed with it.

Everything we have learned so far concerns a fertilized egg, that is, an egg of a hen fertilized by a male rooster, from whose egg a chick can develop, as most eggs were in the past.2

sections.title: Unfertilized Eggs
sections.html:
The forbidden blood in an egg is only blood from which a chick begins to form; therefore, by the letter of the law there is no prohibition in blood found in an egg that is not fertilized, since it is impossible for a chick to develop from it. However, because of mar'it ayin, it must be removed (SA 66:7). Accordingly, there is no obligation to check unfertilized eggs, for only if one happens to see blood in them must it be removed. This phenomenon of blood in an unfertilized egg occurs in one egg out of several thousand eggs sold under supervision.

Today in the State of Israel it is forbidden, for health reasons, to market fertilized eggs for food, since they contain residues of medications injected into the hens that lay them. In practice, more than ninety-seven percent of the eggs marketed for food in Israel are supervised eggs that are not fertilized, and the stamp on them is the sign of this.

Therefore, according to the law, there is no need to check eggs that have a stamp, and if, by chance, while opening the egg, blood is seen in it, it should be removed because of mar'it ayin, and the egg is kosher. Even so, many customarily are meticulous to check all eggs sold in stores, either because they do not know that this is not required, or because they want to be meticulous that the eggs should not contain even blood that is forbidden only because of mar'it ayin.3

sections.title: Honey
sections.html:
Honey is permitted to eat, and indeed the Tanakh relates that Shimshon and Yonatan ate honey. But one must ask: honey is produced by bees, and bees are forbidden to eat as a flying sheretz; how, then, is a food produced by an impure species permitted to eat? After all, we hold the rule: "What comes from the impure is impure," and therefore, for example, the milk of a non-kosher animal is forbidden to eat. Two explanations for this were stated in the Talmud (Bekhorot 7b). According to one opinion (the Tanna Kamma), honey differs from milk, for milk is produced in the animal's body, and if the animal is impure, the milk produced in it is also impure. But honey is not produced in the bees' body; rather, they gather nectar from flowers and plants and store it in their bodies, and afterward discharge it in the hive, and there in the hive the liquids in the nectar evaporate and the honey is formed. And according to another opinion (Rabbi Ya'akov), there is a special derivation from the verse dealing with flying sheratzim, from which one can infer that the honey that comes from bees is kosher.

Beekeepers must strain the honey, because sometimes dead bees, or legs and other body parts of bees, are mixed into the honey. After straining, the honey is kosher. And even if dead bees remained in the honey for a long time, there is no need to be concerned lest they imparted flavor to it, because even if they imparted flavor to it, it is a spoiled flavor (ta'am pagum), which does not forbid (SA YD 81:8; below 34:7).

sections.title: Royal Jelly
sections.html:
Royal jelly is a semi-liquid substance that bees produce from glands in their heads, and its taste is somewhat bitter. By eating large amounts of royal jelly, an ordinary larva develops into the queen bee; otherwise, this larva would become an ordinary bee. The queen bee is unique in that the next generation descends from her: she is capable of laying up to two thousand eggs a day, her weight is double that of the other bees, and her life expectancy is forty times that of the other bees. Since royal jelly is capable of bringing about such extraordinary changes in the bee, there are healers who hold that royal jelly has important medicinal properties.

However, regarding its kashrut the poskim disagreed. Some say that it is forbidden to eat it, because whatever comes from the impure is impure, and since bees are forbidden to eat, the royal jelly they produce from glands in their heads is also forbidden to eat. Its law is not like that of honey, for honey is nectar that the bees gather from flowers and plants and store in the crop located between their mouth and their stomach, and afterward discharge in the hive, and there the nectar dries a little and becomes honey; and since it is processed nectar, honey is permitted to eat. But royal jelly is produced from within the bees' body, and therefore it is forbidden to eat. And even if we say that there is a derivation from the verse that bee honey is kosher, the Torah's intention is to permit only honey, which is known for its taste, but not the other substances secreted by bees.

And some say that its law is like that of honey, for everything that bees produce from their bodies is based on nectar and various kinds of plants that the bees gather. Even honey itself takes its form through the addition of enzymes secreted from glands in the bee's body; and just as honey is kosher, so the other substances that come from the bee's body are kosher. And even if we say that the basis for permitting honey is what is derived from the verse, just as we learned that honey is kosher, so one can learn that all the substances secreted by bees are kosher.

In practice, although it is proper to be concerned for the opinion of the stringent, for medicinal purposes one may be lenient and eat royal jelly, because it is customarily mixed into honey whose quantity is forty times that of the royal jelly, and since its taste is not perceptible, its prohibition is nullified and it is permitted to eat it. Likewise, if it is prepared in the form of tasteless pills, it is permitted to swallow them. And one who is lenient and eats royal jelly as it is should not be rebuked, for he has authorities on whom to rely.4

Bees also produce a substance called propolis, by means of which they protect the hive from contamination and disease; and a substance called pollen, which helps nourish the bees in their youth. It is permitted to eat them, like honey.5
